'How Do Practitioners Build SE Agents? Insights from a Mixed-Methods Study'. arXiv:2607.10856 (v2 stamped 25 Jul 2026). https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10856 (read at https://arxiv.org/html/2607.10856v2). Title/authors confirmed: this IS the paper the docshare.wps.com listing carries, not a different one.

access_status: Read via WebFetch of the arXiv HTML v2; first 100,000 of 118,582 characters read (Sections III to VI). Extraction was done by a summarising model, so quotes should be re-checked against the PDF before publication. Abstract was not reproduced verbatim.

date_and_recency: Posted July 2026 (v2 stamp 25 Jul 2026). Interviews ran February to May 2026 (guide finalised January 2026). Survey dates not stated in the portion read.
key_claims: Study of practitioners who BUILD software engineering agents, not general users of coding assistants. Reports a seven-stage workflow, five process shifts and six challenges with 12 practices. As implementation gets cheaper, bottlenecks shift (requirements, coordination, deployment become more visible), effort moves from producing code to reviewing generated artifacts, and evaluating agent behaviour becomes central. Section V-E frames downstream review burden as 'comprehension debt', linked to 'cognitive debt'.
headline_figures: Interviews n=20 from 12 organisations. Survey n=80 valid of 89. Survey agreement: workflow W1 91%; shifts S1 84%, S2 95% (non-coding work/bottleneck shift), S3 83% (evaluation central), S4 71%, S5 77%; challenges C1 73%, C2 80%, C3 74%, C4 76%, C5 82% (comprehension debt), C6 85%. Practice ratings Very Effective or Essential: regenerability 67.1%; returning maintenance to AI 53.9%. Which survey item maps to 'reviewing' vs 'bottleneck shift' should be confirmed against Table II/III wording.
sample_unit_and_population: Interviews: 12 applied scientists, 3 infrastructure engineers, 5 managers; 15 of 20 from big tech; Asia 9, North America 7, Europe 4; 11 with 5+ years. Survey: Asia 26, North America 17, Europe 15, Africa 13, other 9; mean industry experience 5.0 years; recruited via personal networks, LinkedIn, Prolific. Software practitioners, but skewed to applied scientists building agents.
observed_vs_stated: Stated. Self-reported interviews and survey; no observation of behaviour or physiology.
what_makes_oversight_tiring: Generated code is cheap to produce but hard to comprehend; reviewers inherit volume they cannot fully read ('comprehension debt'). Agents are opaque and nondeterministic, so evaluation is needed to see what they do. Responsibility is pushed to whoever is downstream.
consequence_for_quality: Participants report people giving up reading generated code and burden landing on downstream people. The paper does not quantify defects or errors from this in the portion read. The paper does not use the term 'cognitive load'.
what_reduces_the_load: Preserve regenerability (keep specs, tests, infrastructure rather than a specific implementation; 67.1% rated Very Effective or Essential). Return maintenance to AI (53.9%; authors note this bypasses rather than repays the debt). Move review closer to intent: early checks, human accountability, review surfaces that summarise generated changes (no percentage). Section V-G: practices for comprehension debt got weaker survey support, so it looks unresolved.
limitations_stated: Self-report and builder bias (participants describe agents they built; authors sought failures and kept dissent). Sample skews to big tech (15/20) and applied scientists, may not transfer to smaller firms, non-technical organisations or general users. Data window Feb to May 2026 and tools change fast. Same researchers designed guide and analysed data (confirmation bias). Counts are descriptive; not mentioning a theme is not disagreement. (Section VI, paraphrased from extraction.)
counter_evidence: Survey support for comprehension-debt remedies was weaker than for other practices. Participants are builders, so findings may not describe ordinary developers using agents. Compare with other 2026 preprints seen in search but NOT opened: arXiv 2606.05391 (human oversight of agentic systems in practice), 2609.24234, 2607.07980, 2606.13175 (argues agents supersede human review).
verification_status: Paper opened (arXiv HTML v2): identity, authors, sample sizes, quotes, percentages and limitations checked against it via a summarising fetch tool. Not checked: final 18.5k characters (end of Section VI onward), the PDF, Table II/III item wording, abstract verbatim, funding statement. Other papers listed in counter_evidence: [uncertain], unopened.
usable_claim: In a 2026 interview study (20 practitioners, 12 organisations) and survey (80), people who build software engineering agents reported that as writing code gets cheaper, the effort moves to non-coding work and to reviewing generated code and evaluating agent behaviour. Self-reported, skewed to big tech and applied scientists.
do_not_use: Do not call the sample general developers or agent users. Do not say it measures cognitive load, errors or defects. Do not use the survey percentages as proof that review is the bottleneck without confirming item wording. Do not use agentpatterns.ai's seven-stage summary (secondary, unverified).
